title: CASE OF AKSU v. TURKEY
conclusion: Preliminary objection dismissed (Article 34 - Victim);No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);No violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life)
summary:
In the case of Aksu v. Turkey, the applicant, Mr. Ahmet Aksu, is a Turkish national of Roma origin who brought a complaint against the Turkish state. Mr. Aksu argued that his Roma identity was harmed by the publication of a government-funded book, "The Gypsies of Turkey," and by dictionary definitions that he considered offensive and degrading to Roma and Traveller communities. The core of the case was the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to negative stereotyping and the perpetuation of prejudice through state-supported publications, which Mr. Aksu claimed undermined his dignity and private life.

The events unfolded in 2000, when the Turkish Ministry of Culture published the book in question, which included descriptions and generalisations about Roma people’s physical characteristics and way of life. Mr. Aksu contended that both the book and certain dictionary entries contained language that reflected anti-Roma sentiment and constituted an attack on his identity.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found no violation of Article 8, concluding that the publications did not amount to an unjustified interference with Mr. Aksu’s rights and that there was no evidence of discriminatory intent or effect.

This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights as it clarifies the threshold for state responsibility in cases of alleged group defamation, against a backdrop of historical marginalisation of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe.
